appraisal_events.evidence: « Arbres, pensai-je, vous n'avez plus rien à me dire, mon cœur refroidi ne vous entend plus. [...] Si jamais j'ai pu me croire poète, je sais maintenant que je ne le suis pas. » ; « la pensée de mon absence de dons littéraires [...] me frappa de nouveau et avec une force plus lamentable que jamais »
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage opens by lowering the narrator in his own and the narration's estimation: he confirms his lack of literary gift, registers total indifference before nature, and even convicts his own consolation of worthlessness. The brief lift of memory in the streets toward the Champs-Élysées qualifies but does not reverse this dominantly morne movement, which continues into the demystification of the Guermantes name and of the prince's new house.

appraisal_events.evidence: « M. de Charlus, qui jusque-là n'eût pas consenti à dîner avec Mme de Sainte-Euverte, la saluait maintenant jusqu'à terre » ; « cette nature inaccessible et précieuse [...] M. de Charlus l'anéantit d'un seul coup par la timidité appliquée, le zèle peureux avec lequel il ôta son chapeau » ; « le salut empressé et humble du baron [...] proclamait ce qu'a de périssable l'amour des grandeurs de la terre et tout l'orgueil humain »
appraisal_events.explanation: The stroke-stricken Charlus, reduced to a child under Jupien's care, bows to a woman he formerly judged not chic enough for him, and the narrator explicitly reads the gesture as the annihilation of his aristocratic pride; the duchesse de Létourville's reproachful look and curt « Vous feriez mieux de rentrer », and Jupien's closing revelation about the baron's continued predation, deepen the same fall. The Lear and Bossuet comparisons and the insistence that his intelligence is intact lend the collapse grandeur without reversing it.

status_effects.explanation: He is locally at his lowest: self-declared no poet, incapable of pleasure before the sunlit trees, and aware that his substitute consolation is worthless.
The snobbery that defined his standing is destroyed in a single bow to a woman he had always refused, and a passing duchess treats his condition as a social solecism.
Physical ruin and Jupien's sordid closing anecdote lower him further, though the narrator's elegiac framing and the stress on his unimpaired mind keep this from being total discredit.

She finally receives the homage Charlus had made a point of withholding — « Recevoir l'hommage de M. de Charlus, pour Mme de Sainte-Euverte c'était tout le snobisme » — and is greeted as if she were the queen of France.

ambiguities: The narrator stages several competing causes for Charlus's humble salute (a deliberately meritorious effort, motor incoordination from the stroke, loss of the social code, or genuine detachment from life), so the agency behind the gesture is underdetermined even though its diminishing effect is explicitly asserted.
Mme de Sainte-Euverte's gain is registered only inside a value system the passage treats as vanity ('tout le snobisme'), so her local elevation is real but ironized rather than endorsed.
